The paper designed a radar-absorbing material (RAM) consisting of a Jerusalem cross unit cell based periodic structure bonded with FR4 material, with a total thickness of 6.25 mm.
The proposed RAM design showed more than -10 dB reflection loss from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies.

Three different rivet configurations were studied: (a) rivet installed at the center of a unit cell (RAS C1), (b) rivet installed between the gap of two unit cells (RAS C2), and (c) rivet installed at the center of four unit cells (RAS C3).
The paper studied three cases with varying the percentage of rivet heads area to RAS surface area: (a) 9.8%, (b) 4.4%, and (c) 2.5%.
The results showed that with a reduction in rivet surface area, the degradation in RCS performance was reduced, with the 2.5% case showing a maximum of 3 dB degradation.
An increase in air intake duct length led to an improvement in RCS performance for a given RAS configuration.

For the open-source aircraft CAD model, all the RAS configurations with and without rivets showed almost similar RCS performance, with the RAS configuration providing around 10 dB RCS reduction from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies compared to the non-RAS air intake duct.

The paper noted that the impact of rivets may be more significant on a low-observable aircraft model, and further study on different shapes, sizes, and patterns of rivets installed on air intake ducts is an open research area.
The flat panel RAS sample showed mono-static RCS reduction of 0 dB and 0 dB at normal incidence for horizontal (HH) and vertical (VV) polarizations, respectively.
The mono-static RCS of the flat panel RAS showed good performance even at oblique angles, with RCS reduction observed from -60 to +60 degrees.
The median RCS of the air intake duct showed improvement with an increase in duct length, with the RAS configurations performing better than the metallic (PEC) duct.
Below 4 GHz, the RAS performance was degrading, as the RAS configuration considered in the study was designed to work from 4 to 18 GHz.
The open-source aircraft CAD model showed that the RAS air intake provided around 10 dB RCS reduction from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies compared to the non-RAS air intake duct.
The impact of rivets on the RCS performance of the open-source aircraft CAD model was negligible, as the other components/systems of the aircraft also contributed to the overall RCS.
The paper highlighted that a low RCS aircraft model may show a more significant impact of rivets on the RCS performance, which is an area for future research.
